incidents.title: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.title_en: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.summary:
Angela Lipps, a 50-year-old Tennessee woman, was arrested at gunpoint in July 2025 and jailed for about six months after Fargo, North Dakota police used AI facial recognition to wrongly identify her as a bank fraud suspect. She was held nearly four months in a Tennessee county jail without bail, then about two more months in North Dakota before charges were dropped when her lawyer showed bank records proving she was in Tennessee at the time. Lipps was released on Christmas Eve and later lost her home, car, and belongings.

Lipps is now suing the city of Fargo and detective Lucas Heck for $10 million in federal court, alleging the police relied solely on a flawed facial recognition match from a fake ID and did not investigate further or establish probable cause. The lawsuit claims the department lacked proper policies and training for the technology and that officials have not apologized. Fargo says it does not comment on pending litigation, and the case will proceed in court.

incidents.title: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.title_en: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.summary:
Former Costa Mesa police officer Robert Jay Josett, 35, pleaded guilty to three misdemeanor charges involving unauthorized database access, repeated harassing calls, and violating a restraining order. After his mistress ended their relationship in April 2024, he contacted her thousands of times over nine months, sometimes more than 100 times in one day, and called her and her new boyfriend up to 58 times in a single day. He also made 13 improper searches in a state law enforcement database on his mistress, a romantic rival, and his wife, and used a license plate reader system to track vehicles, including after he was placed on leave.

Josett was served with an emergency protective order and a notice of termination on June 28, 2024, but then drove by the woman's home and was arrested. He was sentenced to three years of informal probation and a 52-week domestic violence program, and he had already spent nine months on a GPS ankle monitor. His law enforcement certification review by California's Peace Officers Standards and Training is pending.

incidents.title: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.title_en: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.summary:
Two sisters from Rio Arriba County are suing Española after police stopped them on July 23. A Flock Safety camera misread their license plate, confusing a final 2 for a 7, and flagged the car as stolen from Rio Rancho. Officers pulled over Jaclynn Gonzales, 21, and her 12-year-old sister on Calle Duran, handcuffed both, and placed them in separate police vehicles before realizing the error. Jaclynn had asked police to call their mother, who lived nearby, but the girl was still handcuffed and detained.

The lawsuits, filed Jan. 3, seek unspecified damages for anxiety, fear, and restriction of movement. Their attorney, Sheri Raphaelson, also represents Adam Pacheco, a 17-year-old honor student who was wrongly stopped in a similar camera-related mistake. The city, police chief, and Flock Safety did not respond to requests for comment. The cases will proceed in state District Court.

incidents.title: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
incidents.title_en: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
incidents.summary:
U.S. intelligence officials say the Russian government has again authorized covert online disinformation operations aimed at November’s midterm elections, seeking to weaken public trust and inflame domestic divisions. The classified assessments found no evidence that Russia tried to compromise voting machines or the actual vote count. Experts have recently identified social media campaigns using artificial intelligence to create fake videos of Hollywood celebrities discussing competitive Senate races. Officials said this operation appears smaller and less coordinated than some past Russian efforts, and Moscow is seen as more focused on presidential elections and distracted by the war in Ukraine.

The activity continues a pattern that U.S. spy agencies say has occurred in every federal election cycle since 2016. It comes as President Trump has repeatedly questioned election integrity, including a July address in which he claimed serious vulnerabilities in U.S. voting systems and accused officials of covering up foreign influence.

incidents.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.title_en: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.summary:
Rebecca Green agreed to have an AI scribe transcribe her first urologist appointment in Australia. After kidney stone surgery, she read a letter from the specialist to her GP that falsely said she micro-dosed psychedelic mushrooms, which she had never done. The error upset her and worried her because she was receiving workers' compensation and feared illegal drug claims could hurt her case. She complained, and the urologist apologised, corrected the record, and said she would review how AI was used in her practice.

A Digital Rights Watch report found similar AI scribe mistakes, including recording the wrong breast in a cancer diagnosis and inventing epilepsy. The Royal Australian College of GPs estimates about 40 percent of GPs regularly use AI scribes. Australia's medicines regulator, the TGA, says no AI scribes are approved and some may be breaking the law. It will release findings in coming weeks and act on breaches. The report calls for approved tools to be tested and published.

reports.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated

incidents.title: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.title_en: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.summary:
A 37 year old Vero Beach man, Peter Solomon Ruma, was arrested and is being held on a one million dollar bond. Police say he used photos from social media and other online sources to create and share AI generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Investigators searched his home and electronic devices on Wednesday and found evidence linking him to the images. He faces eight charges tied to one female victim from June through August 2026, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting them, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Police have identified several other possible victims who may not know images of them were made or shared, and they believe Ruma may have done this for years. He has a prior criminal record, including a 2007 arrest for burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person. The investigation is ongoing and more charges could be filed. Anyone who thinks they were victimized or has information is asked to contact the Vero Beach Police Department. Federal officials recently launched TakeItDown.FTC.gov to help victims report nonconsensual intimate images.

incidents.title: L'homme qui a attaqué une garderie suisse a trouvé ses victimes sur ChatGPT
incidents.title_en: The man who attacked a Swiss daycare found his victims on ChatGPT
incidents.summary:
On 1 October 2024, a 23-year-old Chinese student attacked three five-year-old boys outside a childcare centre in Zurich Oerlikon with a knife whose blade was about 8.5 centimetres long. One boy had a major vein at his collarbone completely severed and needed emergency surgery, another was stabbed twice in the chest and nearly died from heart and blood vessel injuries, and the third suffered wounds to his ear and lung. A childcare worker grabbed the attacker's arms, he dropped the knife and surrendered, and passersby held him until police arrived.

Prosecutors say the man, who had come to Switzerland a year earlier for a master's degree, planned the attack for weeks. He used ChatGPT to ask about legal consequences of stabbing random victims, ordered clothes and kitchen knives, studied anatomy, and bought raw beef to practise stabbing. He chose 1 October, China's national day, and posted patriotic content online shortly before the attack. At his trial on Thursday, the prosecution is seeking a 15-year prison sentence and a 15-year expulsion from Switzerland.

Parkview High School in Gwinnett County, Georgia received its fourth AI-generated bomb threat of the school year on Monday, according to Gwinnett Schools Police. The school was placed on lockdown out of an abundance of caution, and it later returned to normal operations. The latest threat involved a masked phone number, matching a pattern seen in recent incidents.

Gwinnett County school police are now working with the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the FBI to determine who is responsible. No arrests have been made and no suspect has been identified. The article does not state what specific steps will follow, but the investigation is ongoing.

stories.Headline: Trump to rename AI into SI 'Super Intelligence'
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced at the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026 that he is ordering the term “Artificial Intelligence” to be replaced with “Super Intelligence,” or SI, in all official U.S. documents. He told world leaders that the word “artificial” makes the technology sound fake, when he believes it is actually amazing, and that “super” is more accurate. He also rejected any global plan to regulate AI, saying the United States must not fall behind China in an AI arms race.

The article notes that “super intelligence” already exists as an industry term for AI that surpasses human intelligence, and it is both a goal for many companies and a concern for critics. Trump said that from now on, U.S. documents, and hopefully those of other countries, will use the new name. No further steps or timeline were given beyond this announcement.

stories.Headline: Sen. Bernie Sanders unveils bill to ban artificial superintelligence and create Department of AI - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar introduced a bill to permanently ban artificial superintelligence, meaning any system that exceeds human cognitive ability or could plan humanity's destruction. It would pause advanced AI development until a new Department of Artificial Intelligence sets safety rules, then require federal approval before deployment. Violations could bring up to 20 years in prison. Some employees at OpenAI and Google DeepMind support the bill.

The bill faces long odds in the Republican-controlled Congress, where even less sweeping AI rules have stalled. President Trump has resisted oversight, while some tech leaders warn of catastrophic risks. Public concern is rising, with 53 percent of Americans now extremely or very worried about AI's environmental impact, up from 41 percent last year. Sanders says avoiding dangerous AI will require cooperation with China, like Cold War nuclear arms control.

stories.Headline: Vyzoxa Redefines AI Learning Through Practical AI Agent Development, Empowering Learners Worldwide to Build With Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Vyzoxa, an education technology platform run by NDFM Business World Pvt. Ltd., has introduced a practical artificial intelligence learning pathway. It aims to help one million people become AI innovators by 2030. Participants first complete about two weeks of AI agent industrial training with recorded lessons and daily tasks. They then move into a four week project based internship in AI agent development at no extra cost, where they build and present a working AI agent. The program is remote and self paced, open to learners in India and many international regions.

The platform includes AI tools called Vyzoxa Intelligent Systems, such as an AI mentor, AI coder, and AI engine, to support learning and project work. Founder Mansajan Singh and Managing Director Gurjinder Singh lead the company. For eligible participants in India, top performers may be shortlisted for a final interview and could receive employment or pre-placement offers, but these are performance based and not guaranteed. The article does not state a specific next step beyond the platform's ongoing mission and enrollment.

stories.Headline: Gov. Pritzker Establishs Illinois Artificial Intelligence (AI) Cabinet - Forth.News
stories.Summary:
Governor JB Pritzker signed Executive Order 2026-07 to create an Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet. This group will include experts from academia, law, ethics, governance, and state agencies such as emergency management, public health, and technology. It will assess risks AI poses to residents, advise on preparing for and responding to AI incidents, and recommend safeguards for public buildings, water systems, and information infrastructure. The order follows earlier state AI safety laws and comes amid federal inaction and a recent whistleblower resignation.

The cabinet will also evaluate possible regulatory steps, including tying data center tax incentives to safety standards, addressing energy burdens on the grid, and considering strict liability for AI caused harm. Governor Pritzker will seek input from agency leaders and announce appointed members in the coming weeks. Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Chancellor Charles Isbell voiced support.

stories.Headline: Banks Warn AI Shopping Bots Raise Scam, Fraud and Data-Privacy Risks
stories.Summary:
A group of banks, including NatWest, Bank of America, ING, Capital One, ASB Bank, and Commonwealth Bank of Australia, warned on September 22 that AI shopping agents could increase scams, fraud, and data privacy breaches. They noted that technology firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta are promoting chatbots to select products and buy on behalf of shoppers. British retailer John Lewis said AI agent searches grew to 2.5 percent from 0.3 percent a year earlier. The banks said customers are interested but the technology is moving faster than consumer protections.

The report highlighted risks such as AI agents taking card details and entering them directly into websites, or pushing users toward payment methods with weaker safeguards. Consumers worry about wrong purchases, overspending, or losing money to fraud, and are unsure who would help. The banks plan to discuss proposals with policymakers, including requiring disclosure when an AI agent is involved, more transparency about how agents decide, safeguards for customer data, and allowing consumers and merchants to choose interoperable AI shopping services.

stories.Headline: Pritzker establishes AI cabinet amid calls for greater regulation
stories.Summary:
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed an executive order on Tuesday creating an artificial intelligence cabinet made up of unpaid experts and state agency representatives. The group will develop policy proposals through 2027 and examine risks AI poses to residents and critical infrastructure such as water systems, education, and information networks. It will also study emerging AI incidents and recommend safety, accountability, and transparency measures, including possible conditions on data center incentives and reviews of energy grid strain.

The move follows a whistleblower's claim that AI could become uncontrollable by 2030, and it builds on Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act signed in July. That law targets AI models earning over $500 million annually, requires reporting on risks like weapons creation or cyberattacks, and mandates annual audits starting in 2028. Pritzker is urging Congress to hold hearings and set national standards, saying AI is as dangerous as nuclear weapons and needs international cooperation.

stories.Headline: Australia AI regulations: Anthropic, OpenAI call for Australia to relax ban on training of AI models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI and Anthropic have asked Australia to soften its planned ban on using local creative content to train artificial intelligence models. The two US companies made submissions to a parliamentary inquiry in September, arguing that a narrow copyright exemption could protect creators while attracting investment. Australia has already ruled out such an exemption, and its broader AI and data centre rules take effect next year. The companies say the sector could be worth hundreds of billions of dollars by the end of the decade.

Anthropic proposed a conditional approval system and said it would consider conditions that support Australian creators. OpenAI called for a balanced framework allowing models to learn from information that is publicly available while giving rightsholders chances to collaborate. Both companies linked their requests to major local projects, including an OpenAI data centre deal in Sydney and an Anthropic partnership in Queensland. The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence is due to report in November.

stories.Headline: Why are privacy fears threatening the future of AI glasses?
stories.Summary:
AI-powered wearables, especially Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses, are facing privacy lawsuits and restrictions. Consumers are suing Meta and Luxottica, claiming human reviewers saw recordings of people changing clothes or using bathrooms after footage was uploaded to train AI. UK venues including Wetherspoon have limited use of the frames. Meta says a light that cannot be turned off during filming protects bystanders and denies the allegations. Samsung plans to enter smart glasses later this year with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but does not see them as smartphone replacements.

Startups are responding with camera-free or consent-based designs. Even Realities, valued at $1 billion, expects a few hundred thousand users for its camera-free glasses. Pocket has about 170,000 phone-mounted recorders that require a button press, and Plaud has 2.5 million users and over $100 million in annual recurring revenue with earbuds that alert bystanders. OpenAI's Sam Altman says always-on devices need local data processing, which may take a couple of years. Meta is expected to unveil camera-free smart glasses as early as Wednesday at its Connect conference.

stories.Headline: Privacy Commissioner puts Manage My Health, Health NZ on notice after data breach
stories.Summary:
The Privacy Commissioner has issued formal compliance notices to Health New Zealand and the patient portal Manage My Health after a December 2025 cyber attack on the portal. Hackers leaked data belonging to almost 100,000 people, about 90 percent of them in Northland. The stolen files included 403,730 Health New Zealand documents and 22,609 documents uploaded by patients. An earlier investigation found both organisations failed to have adequate security controls under the Health Information Privacy Code.

Commissioner Michael Webster said the notices require the two bodies to meet security obligations and give patients confidence their data is being protected. Manage My Health has already improved multifactor authentication and restricted unauthorised access. It must complete all required changes by the end of August 2027, while Health New Zealand has until the end of January. Webster noted the impact on Māori in Northland, where most affected patients live.

stories.Headline: Virginia governor presses Congress for AI guardrails
stories.Summary:
Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger sent a letter to top congressional leaders, including House Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune, urging them to set national rules for artificial intelligence. She warned that leaving oversight mainly to private companies could threaten jobs, privacy, and public resources. Spanberger also announced state-level steps, such as a data center accountability framework and an executive order creating an AI task force, but she did not propose specific federal legislation or give a timetable for recommendations.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 73 percent of Americans believe AI companies have not done enough to prevent serious harm, while 55 percent support slowing AI development and 13 percent oppose it. Last year, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to remove a provision that would have discouraged states from regulating AI. Representative Don Beyer and ten other House members also pressed for federal action. Congress remains divided, and Johnson has said he will not rush to regulate, so no immediate federal legislation is certain.
